BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, 2-D art and sound assets, 34 terms for getting a picture or a sound to work inside a Godo game, from pixels and frames to import settings, loops and the mix. With the exact term, you can tell an AI coding agent what to fix.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in For Bear. Newcomers often think an image resolution is the size the game shows it at. It is not. Resolution is only the pixels in the file. The game draws into its own viewport and the file has to be scaled to fit it. This film goes through the terms group by group, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Eight labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Editor or docs, the term comes from the editor itself or its official documentation. Video only, the term comes from a video lecture and is not in the course text or on the term list, computed. The numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Simulation, a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea not measured. Conceptual, a drawing of the idea with no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map 34 terms and 4 groups each about getting a picture or a sound to work inside the engine. The first group is size and pixels. Resolution, viewport, aspect ratio, uniform versus non-uniform, texel, nearest versus linear and integer scaling.

B0102.heard: The second group is frames and cutouts, sprite sheet, texture atlas, sprite frames, frame rate, alpha channel, transparent background, PNG versus JPEG, two image file formats and fringe. These terms say how frames are cut from an image and how their edges stay clean.

B0103.heard: The third group is import, readability, and collider. Import settings, lossless versus lossy, mipmaps, silhouette, readability, and collider. These terms say what the engine does to a file and what the player actually sees.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is Sound PCM, which is raw audio samples, sample rate, Nyquist limit, procedural synthesis, WAV versus Ogg Vorbis, two sound file formats, loop point, one shot, audio stream player, polyphony, bus, decibel, headroom and clipping. They say how a sound is stored, loop, played and mixed.

B0201.heard: On the left is an image file, a red circle drawn at half size. Resolution is the width and height of an image in pixels. It is a fact about the file, not about the game. This file is 1024 by 873, which makes 893,952 pixels. For example, a picture of termite soldiers that an image model made for an enemy arrived at exactly that resolution. Far bigger than the game would ever draw it.

B0202.heard: Beside the file at the same scale is the red box of the viewport, the area the game draws into. It is set in project settings and the window scales it. Resolution is pixels in the file and the viewport is pixels the game draws into. Here the file is 1.6 times wider and 2.42 times taller. For example the Walker game draws into a 640x360 viewport, stretched to fill its window.

B0203.heard: Now both rectangles are drawn the same height. Aspect ratio is width divided by height, the shape of a rectangle whatever its size. The image comes to 1.17 nearly square. The viewport comes to 1.78 wide. The ratios differ so no single scale makes the image fill the viewport exactly. For example a title screen painted nearly square cannot fill a wide game window without bars at the sides or a stretched picture.

B0204.heard: Two ways to shrink the file into the viewport. Uniform versus non-uniform is the choice between one scale factor on both axes and different factors that distort. On the left, two factors squash the circle into an ellipse. On the right, one factor, the smaller 0.412 keeps the circle round and leaves bars at the sides. For example, a character portrait for a dialogue box should be scaled uniformly, or the face comes out stretched sideways.

B0301.heard: This is a small invented sprite, 6x6, drawn as a grid. A texel is one pixel of a texture, counted inside the image before the engine draws it. This sprite stores 36 texels, and the red square marks one of them, a white texel with the value zero. For example, a coin icon stored as a tiny grid of texels still holds exactly those texels when the camera zooms in, even though each one now covers many screen pixels.

B0302.heard: The same sprite drawn four times larger in two ways. Nieris versus linear names two ways the engine fills screen pixels from texels. Nieris takes one texel and keeps hard edges. Liner blends four and smooths them. On the left, Nieris keeps two shades. On the right, Liner makes 24. Every extra one a gray the artist never drew. For example, Godo's project default is linear. So a pixel art enemy looks soft until its sprite node is set to nearest.

B0303.heard: Three rows show how wide each sprite pixel lands on screen. Integer scaling means enlarging by whole numbers, so every pixel of pixel art stays the same width. At scale 2, every pixel is 2 screen pixels wide, and at scale 3, all are 3. At 2.5 widths alternate, so some are 50% wider. For example, the Walker game stretches its viewport to a window exactly twice as wide and twice as tall. So each game pixel becomes a clean block.

B0401.heard: One image file cut into four equal cells of 48 by 48 pixels, each holding a bug. A sprite sheet is one image that holds many frames in a grid. This file is 192 by 48 pixels, and because the cells are equal, a test can count them. The sprite sheet is the image, and sprite frames is the resource that plays it, for example. A hero's run cycle, generated as one row of poses in a single PNG file, is a sprite sheet.

B0402.heard: Now the last cell is lit and its bug is cut out below. A texture atlas is many small images packed into one big texture, each picture a region, a rectangle of it. Godot cuts a frame as an atlas texture, the sheet plus that rectangle. Here the region starts 144 pixels across and zero down, 48 wide and 48 tall. For example, the coin, heart and key icons on a game score bar can share one atlas. Each drawn from its own rectangle.

B0403.heard: A text box lists one animation and the bug plays beside it. Sprite Frames is a Godot resource that holds named animations, each with its frames, a speed and a loop flag. This one is named Walk, plays frames 0 to 3 at 5 FPS frames per second and loops. 5 FPS is what a new animation gets by default. For example, in Walker's termite exercise the agent wrote a Sprite Frames file with one animation for each soldier. Named by Head Color.

B0404.heard: The same four frames played side by side at two speeds. Frame rate is how many frames are shown each second. At five FPS, one walk cycle takes 0.8 seconds. At twelve FPS, it takes 0.33 seconds. The frames are the same and only the pace changes. For example, a beetle enemy that seems to scurry too fast can be calmed down by lowering the frame rate of its walk animation with no new art at all.

B0501.heard: A strip shows one pixel at nine opacities, from see-through on the left to solid on the right. The alpha channel is the extra channel after red, green, and blue that stores how opaque each pixel is. Zero is fully see-through and one is fully solid. Alpha is a value stored in the file. For example, a ghost enemy drawn with its body at alpha 0.5 lets the level behind its show-through.

B0502.heard: Two versions of the same dark sprite. A transparent background means the pixels around the art really are alpha zero, a true cutout. On the left, a model asked for transparent painted a checkerboard so the corner pixel is alpha one. On the right, the art was made on solid gray, then cut, so the corner is alpha zero. For example, Walker's own art notes say never to prompt for transparent background because the generator bakes in a checkerboard.

B0503.heard: Rose of boxes show the channels each file type stores per pixel. PNG versus JPEG is the choice between a lossless file that keeps alpha and a lossy file with no alpha at all. The PNG stores red, green, blue and alpha. The JPEG stores only the first three, so its memory bar is shorter. For example, the termite reference image arrived as a JPEG with a white background, so a sprite cut straight from it would keep a white box around the creature.

B0504.heard: Two strip sample one sprite edge over a dark red level. Fringe or halo is the pale rim of edge color left around a cutout. Filtering blends in the color stored in the see-through pixels. Stored as white, the lightest sample is 0.44, a pale halo. With fixed alpha border and import option that stores the edge color there, it is 0.29. For example, a dark enemy cut from white shows a pale outline whenever that option is off.

B0601.heard: A chain of three boxes, your file, a text file beside it, and a cache. Import settings are the options for one asset that control how Godot converts it, kept in a text file ending in .import next to the source. Godot never uses your PNG or WAV directly. Commit the import file, not the .godot cache folder, for example because the import file is plain text. An agent's test can check that a new sprite was imported lossless with mipmaps off.

B0602.heard: In this simulated row of 24 pixels, lossless versus lossy is the choice between an exact copy of every pixel in a smaller file that loses detail. The lossless row keeps every pixel, so its average error is zero. The modeled lossy row stores one average for every four pixels, and its error is zero point four. Single pixel details go first. For example, a pixel art bat whose eyes or single pixels should be imported lossless. Or the eyes smear into its face.

B0603.heard: Bars show a texture of 256 by 256 and its shrunk copies. MIP maps are pre-shrunk copies of a texture, each half the size of the last used when it is drawn small. All nine sizes cost about 33% more memory. Drawn a quarter size, the engine uses the 64 by 64 copy. A sprite drawn at its own size does not need them, for example. Turn MIP maps on for a painted backdrop. The camera zooms far out from.

B0701.heard: An invented bug once in color and once filled black. A silhouette is the outline of an object on its own. The test is to fill it black at game size and ask whether the shape still says what it is. Color and detail are gone and what is left is what the player notices first. For example, before accepting a generated spider enemy, fill it black and check that its legs and body still make a spider, not a blob.

B0702.heard: The bug at three sizes and the smallest magnified six times. Readability is how well a character can be understood in the game's real view at its real size. Shrinking 436 pixels to 48 puts 9.08 source pixels into each sprite pixel, so a leg 4 pixels wide becomes 0.44 of a pixel, a faint smear. For example, judge a new termite enemy beside the player in the running level. Not in an image viewer.

B0801.heard: In this made up example, a character's art, the pink box with arms, sits around a red dashed box. A collider is the shape used for contact tests separate from the art and sized from the body. Here it is 18 by 28 pixels and the art reaches 12 pixels past each side. The collider counts as solid, the art is what the player sees. For example, the Walker player collides as an 18 by 28 box, while its wide mascot art reaches past it.

B0802.heard: Now the art is flipped and the little flag points left, but the dashed box has not moved. Keep the collider a sibling of the sprite node, not its child. If it were a child, mirroring or scaling the art would change the collider too. For example, when the player turns to run left, the code flips only the sprite, and the collision box stays exactly where it was.

B0803.heard: A spike comes in from the right, it overlaps the art for 12 pixels before it touches the collider and counts as a hit. That gap is a design choice. Art past the box is fair if it is thin or decorative and unfair if it looks like the part that hurts. Right down Y. For example, a termite enemies box can cover only its head and body, so its thin legs and antennae brush the player without a hit.

B0901.heard: Stem's mark one cycle of a tone. PCM pulse code modulation is uncompressed digital audio, a plain list of numbers, one per sample, each between minus one and one. Here a 440 Hz tone at 22,050 samples a second has one cycle lasting 2.27 milliseconds, and every stem is one number in the list, for example. A jump sound imported from a WAV file with compression turned off is stored as PCM.

B0902.heard: The same tone sampled at two rates. Sample rate is how many audio samples are stored each second. At 22,050 a second one cycle gets about 50 samples and the curve is smooth. At 2,000 a second it gets 4.5, a crude copy, the red zigzag. For example, Godo's generator demo fills its sound buffer at 22,050 samples a second, so each second of its tone is that many numbers.

B0903.heard: A chart of the pitch heard against the pitch played at 22,050 samples a second. The Nyquist limit is the highest frequency a sample rate can hold half the rate here 11,025 Hertz. Above it a pitch folds back down so a 15,000 Hertz tone is heard as 7,050. The sample rate counts samples and the Nyquist limit is half of it. For example a pickup chime synthesized above that limit plays at a wrong. Lower pitch.

B0904.heard: Line of code, its formula, and the first six values. Procedural synthesis is sound made by a formula evaluated one sample at a time, with no file and no model. Each row moves the phase on a little and takes its sign zero, then 0.1251 and so on. It is not a recording and not a generative model. For example, Walker's audio generator plays a 440 Hz tone this way, with no sound file at all.

B1001.heard: A made-up waveform stands for a four-second music loop at 44,100 samples a second. WAV versus OGG-Vorbis is a choice of sound file. WAV suits short effects and OGG-Vorbis suits music's speech and long sounds. Their loop settings differ. A WAV counts loop begin and end in samples, and an OGG has only one start offset. For example, a game's jump sound ships as a WAV. In its long background, song is an OGG-Vorbis file.

B1002.heard: Markers now sit at both ends joined by an arrow. A loop point is where a looping sound jumps back to. For this WAV the loop mode is forward from sample zero to sample 176,399, the last sample of the four seconds. At the end playback jumps back to the loop begin so the ends must match. For example a menu song can set its loop begin after a short intro so the intro plays only once. //

B1003.heard: Two lanes play together, one shot means a sound plays once and stops. The music loop set to forward goes round again. The jump sound with looping disabled finishes once and stops. A one shot ends so its finished signal arrives and a loop never ends so that signal never comes. For example, in Walker's audio exercise the jump and fail sounds were meant to be one shots but the first try left their loop mode undetected.

B1004.heard: Two seams where the loop's end meets at start again. Cut partway through a cycle. The wave jumps by 0.22 a full scale and you hear a click. Cut where the wave crosses zero, the jump is zero, and there's no click. Start and end the loop on a zero crossing, then listen across the seam three times. For example, a looping engine hum for a race car that ticks once every time round was cut off a zero crossing.

B1101.heard: A chain from a sound file through a player node to the master bus. Audio Stream Player is the Godot node that plays one sound stream with no position in the world, so it suits music and interface sounds. Calling play sends the stream onto a bus. Audio Stream Player 2D pans and fades with position instead. For example, a menu's button sound belongs on a plain audio stream player. While a waterfall that grows louder as the player walks near belongs on Audio Stream Player 2D. Audio Stream Player 3D

B1102.heard: A timeline of three play calls 40 milliseconds apart on a 60 millisecond click. Polyphony is how many copies of one sound can play at once and Go-Dose default is one. With one voice each new play cuts off the last so you hear 40, 40 then 60 milliseconds a stutter. For example a coin sound on a single voice player cuts itself short when the player grabs three coins in quick succession.

B1103.heard: Now the player is allowed four voices. Each sound is heard in full 60 milliseconds and neighbors overlap by 20. There is a second fix in the event rather than the file. Play the sound only on the transition into a state not on every frame the state is true. For example the rhythm game's hit sound player is set to four voices so fast perfect and good hits each play whole.

B1201.heard: Two players feed two buses, which feed master. A bus is a channel that sounds are routed through for shared volume and effects. Each bus can be lowered, duct or muted on its own, so levels are set in the mix, not the file. Here the music player sits at minus 12 decibels on bus music, and the effects player at zero on bus SFX for sound effects. For example, a settings menu's music slider lowers the music bus and leaves the jumps alone.

B1202.heard: A ladder of decibel values beside their amplitudes. A decibel is a logarithmic unit of loudness. Every minus six decibels about half the amplitude, so minus six is 0.501, minus 20 is 0.1, and minus 60 is 0.001. The scale stays short. For example, the rhythm game sets its song player to minus 12 decibels, 0.251 of full amplitude.

B1203.heard: A sine wave sits under a line marked maximum level, 1.0. Headroom is the spare level left between a sound's peak and the maximum. This peak is 0.5, which is minus 6.02 decibels, so the headroom is 6.02 decibels. That space is kept for loud moments. For example, a mix that leaves headroom lets an explosion land on top of the music without reaching the maximum.

B1204.heard: The same sign turned up by 7.6 decibels. Clipping is the distortion when a signal goes past the maximum level. The peak would reach 1.2 so the tops are cut flat, here on 37.2% of the samples and you hear a crackle. Headroom is level left below the maximum and clipping is level past it. For example, a boss roar boosted on a bus that is already loud loses its peaks and crackles through the speakers.

B1301.heard: Each pair sets two look alike terms side by side. Resolution is the pixels in the image file. Here, 1,024 by 873. The viewport is the pixels the game draws into. 640 by 360.

B1302.heard: MIP maps are pre-shrunked copies of one texture, chosen by how big it appears on screen here for sizes. Filtering is how one sample is taken from a texture, nearest or linear. Linear blends four texels.

B1303.heard: Sample rate counts audio samples per second, 22,050, too many to draw. Frame rate counts animation frames per second, five here and everyone is visible. One belongs to sound, the other to pictures.

B1304.heard: A loop point is where playback jumps back to so the sound goes round again. A one shot plays once and stops. Background music loops and a jump sound is a one shot.

B1401.heard: On the left, a vague request above the exact instruction that replaces it. Make the art fit the game becomes, scale the image by one factor, 0.412 on both axes, two factors stretch at 1.52 to 1, one factor keeps the shape.

B1402.heard: Make the pixels crisp becomes, set the filter to nearest on the sprite node and import lossless with mipmaps off. After enlarging four times, linear shows 24 shades and nearest only two. It adds no new colors.

B1403.heard: The walk is too fast becomes, set the walk animation in sprite frames from 12 to 6 FPS. One 4 frame cycle then takes 0.67 seconds. Cycle time is frames divided by FPS.

B1404.heard: Make the music loop becomes, import the music loop file with loop mode forward, begin zero, and 176,399, cut on a zero crossing. Both ends sit on zero, so there's no click.

B1405.heard: The effect is too loud and crackles becomes lower the SFX bus by six decibels. A peak of 1.2 becomes 0.6 under the maximum of 1 and nothing clips.

B1501.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before a generated asset goes into the game. First, is the image scaled by one factor to the viewport with its shape kept.

B1502.heard: Second is the background alpha zero at the corners, with no halo and no painted checkerboard. Check the corner pixels themselves, not a thumbnail.

B1503.heard: Third is the filter nearest on the node with mipmaps off and a lossless import. The filter belongs to the node and the other two belong to the import file.

B1504.heard: Fourth, do the frame count, the layout and the speed match the sprite frames. A test can count frames, but only you can tell a new pose from a different creature.

B1505.heard: Fifth is the collider sized from the body and kept as a sibling of the sprite so that flipping the art never moves it.

B1506.heard: Sixth is the sound imported with the right loop mode played once per event at a safe level. Then say it exactly. Not make it crisp, but nearest on the node, lossless, no mipmaps.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap, resolution is pixels in the file, the viewport is pixels the game draws into. Pixel art needs nearest on the node and whole number scaling. A sprite sheet is the image and sprite frames is the resource that plays it. Cut the background to alpha zero and never prompt for transparent one. The collider is sized from the body and kept apart from the art. A loop point repeats, a one shot stops, and headroom keeps a mix from clipping.

BHTF.heard: Give me short cases for making a 2D game one at a time about its art and sound. Each case should turn on one of these terms, resolution, viewport, nearest versus linear, sprite sheet, sprite frames, mip maps, loop point, one shot, headroom, or clipping. I must name the exact term and say why its look alike is wrong. Wait for my reply before you give the answer.

BOUT.heard: Key terms 2D art and sound assets at Nick Bear Brown.
